raw_response:
# A Q&A framework shortlist

**Question2Answer is the strongest first prototype for the stated PHP/MySQL preference.** It already addresses much of the core Q&A model, while Askbot is the most useful complete alternative found if Python is acceptable. I would evaluate the remaining requirements as concrete integrations before choosing a platform.

The decision date is **28 February 2014**. The sources below mix dated historical releases and current documentation. I distinguish them because a present-day feature list cannot establish what was available in 2014. These are candidates for evaluation; none has been deployed or tested in this research.

## Ranked candidates

### 1. Question2Answer — primary framework

[Official documentation](https://docs.question2answer.org/) describes PHP/MySQL, categories and tags, voting, reputation points, translation, differentiated user roles and plugin customization. That is a strong match to the preferred stack and core community workflow.

The [dated version history](https://docs.question2answer.org/install/versions/1/) establishes version 1.6.3 on 19 January 2014. Its 2013 entries document question view counters, per-category privileges, moderation based on points, uploaded-content storage and an image-upload API. They also document security fixes and CSRF protection. This supports treating Q2A as a real pre-decision candidate, while avoiding the assumption that every modern feature existed then.

I would still verify arbitrary file attachments, mathematics authoring, badge compatibility and reporting. Image upload is narrower than accepting arbitrary attachments; a view counter is narrower than a weekly operational dashboard. The project's scaling and security descriptions are useful leads, but do not establish capacity or security under a particular workload.

### 2. Askbot — complete Python/Django alternative

[Askbot](https://www.askbot.com/) is worth comparing when Python is an acceptable development stack. Its current official site describes tags, voting, accepted answers, reputation-based privileges, badges, moderation and a multilingual interface.

There is useful historical evidence: [Askbot 0.7.49 on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/askbot/0.7.49/) was released on 19 September 2013. Its version-specific description confirms votes, reputation, user levels and combined text/tag search, and identifies the software as GPLv3. That package recommends PostgreSQL and specifies old Django/Python requirements and a MyISAM constraint for MySQL.

This makes Askbot a concrete historical alternative, but it does not prove that the old version covered every requested feature. Mathematics, attachments, badges and reporting deserve version-specific checks. Integrating it into an existing Django application also had documented limitations.

### 3. Question2Answer Badges plugin — fill the gamification gap

The [Q2A Badges plugin](https://github.com/NoahY/q2a-badges) provides configurable achievement badges, award notifications and badge displays on profiles and posts. Its README also describes translation and hooks for custom badges. This is a direct extension of the first candidate, rather than a separate forum.

The README labels it beta. Compatibility with the selected Q2A release and the required award rules needs verification. I did not establish a dated release before February 2014, so its historical availability remains unknown.

### 4. Drupal Answers — modular CMS alternative

[Drupal Answers](https://www.drupal.org/project/answers) assembles questions and answers with supporting accepted-answer, voting, reputation and tagging modules. It is worth considering when the project also needs a broader CMS and the developer is willing to assemble the workflow.

The present project page warns about incompatible version changes and reports no supported stable releases. I could not verify a dated historical feature snapshot, so this is an architecture alternative with substantial integration and version-selection caveats.

### 5. AnswerHub — commercial comparison point

[AnswerHub's official developer documentation](https://developer.answerhub.com/) describes role-based permissions, moderation, built-in badges and reputation, plus REST APIs, plugins and themes. Those capabilities make it relevant to a purchase-versus-development comparison.

I did not verify pricing or a complete match for mathematical editing, multilingual operation, attachments and reporting. A targeted demonstration and written feature scope would be needed to judge whether paying reduces enough implementation work. The live documentation does not establish the exact feature set offered in February 2014.

### 6. Q2A WYSIWYG Math Editor — later mathematical-authoring component

The [Q2A WYSIWYG Math Editor repository](https://github.com/fardina/q2a-wysiwyg-matheditor) shows a CKEditor-based approach to editing mathematical formulas and rendering them with MathJax. It is a relevant implementation path for the LaTeX-oriented authoring requirement.

The inspected README explicitly discusses a September 2019 update and testing with Q2A 1.8.2. This is **post-decision evidence**, not proof of an available solution in February 2014. Version compatibility and the exact editor/rendering integration still need checking.

## How I would evaluate the choice

For Q2A, I would build a small representative workflow: create a tagged question, post and accept an answer, vote, earn reputation, exercise moderator permissions, upload the required file types and author a realistic formula. Then I would produce the requested weekly answer count and page-visit report. These are proposed acceptance checks, not completed tests.

The [official Q2A plugin catalogue](https://docs.question2answer.org/addons/plugins/) confirms that extension routes exist for badges and mathematics, but its live entries do not date those routes to 2014. Translation of interface text also needs to be distinguished from a community containing multiple content languages. Ease of development and scalability depend on the chosen version, plugins, hosting and actual workload; the reviewed sources do not settle those questions.

A public unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt was inaccessible. I therefore used **code-through-web** discovery of public GitHub repositories, not a successful native code-search session. I also inspected OSQA's public repository, but did not obtain enough dated feature evidence to rank it above the six candidates here.
